analysis.one_liner: Lets the government license generic copies of overpriced or shelved patented medicines and requires drugmakers to disclose pricing costs.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in two House committees until the Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let the Secretary of Health and Human Services authorize generic production of a patented medicine when the patent holder is not making it available, cannot meet health needs, or charges more than reasonable pricing criteria allow. Patent holders would still be paid for any licensed use. It would also require every maker of a still-patented drug to file an annual audited report to Congress on its pricing and research costs, and cut off Medicare and Medicaid payments to any company that refuses to file.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who pay for patented prescription drugs, including Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries and their programs, if compulsory licensing or the threat of it lowers prices or makes unavailable medicines accessible. Generic drug makers would gain a lawful channel to produce copies of overpriced patented drugs while paying the patent holder.

how_it_helps.text: The Secretary of Health and Human Services could authorize nonexclusive, nonassignable use of a patented health invention when the patent holder has not put the invention into practical use, has not met health or safety needs, or prices it above criteria set by the Secretary of Commerce, with the right holder paid adequate remuneration in each case.

Every maker of a still-patented drug would have to report to Congress annually a full audit of the financial information relevant to that drug's pricing, including research and development costs, giving the public and lawmakers an evidentiary basis for judging prices.

A company that fails to file the pricing audit would become ineligible for federal payments, including Medicare and Medicaid, for its drugs until it complies, giving the disclosure requirement real teeth.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies would bear the cost: they could lose exclusive control of patents whose products are overpriced or underused, would have to open their pricing and research books to an annual audit, and could lose federal drug revenue entirely for noncompliance.

drawbacks.text: Compulsory licensing weakens the patent exclusivity that drug companies say funds research into new medicines; a license authorized because a drug is priced above federal criteria would let competitors sell it while the patent holder collects only court-reviewed remuneration, and critics argued this would reduce incentives to develop drugs in the first place.

The bill gives the Secretaries of Health and Human Services and Commerce sweeping discretion to define 'reasonably expected' pricing and 'health or safety needs', which would invite prolonged litigation over every determination and could make the licensing power unpredictable in practice.

Companies that miss a filing deadline would be cut off from all federal drug payments, a penalty so severe that an inadvertent late report could disrupt Medicare and Medicaid supply of a drug until the Secretary finds compliance.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacks the core of high drug prices — patent-protected pricing with no public accounting — by pairing a government backstop on abusive pricing with mandatory disclosure, and it preserves compensation for patent holders rather than taking patents outright. The trade-off is real: weaker exclusivity could mean somewhat less private research investment, and the pricing criteria and audit rules would be litigated heavily. On balance it offered patients a direct lever against drug prices that the law at the time did not provide.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Judiciary and Commerce committees and their subcommittees in October 1999, and no committee ever acted on it before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Sherrod Brown of Ohio introduced the bill on September 23, 1999, joined by ten cosponsors including Rep. Bernie Sanders, an Independent.

It was referred to both the Judiciary and Commerce committees on the day of introduction and, within two weeks, to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Courts and Intellectual Property and the Commerce Subcommittee on Health and Environment.
The last action in the record is a sponsor's introductory remark on March 21, 2000; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers came out ahead: they kept exclusive patent control over their medicines and never had to open their pricing and research costs to an annual audit, so patients continued paying unexamined prices. The compulsory-licensing and disclosure powers never took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers and patent holders

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered repeated floor statements urging its consideration between September 1999 and March 2000.

against.role: Brand-name drug makers and their trade association
against.what_they_did: Opposed government price-review and compulsory-licensing proposals of this kind as threats to patent exclusivity and research funding during the 106th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; all 12 sponsors were Democrats or the Independent Bernie Sanders, and the Republican chairs of both referred committees took no action, so any partisan split can only be inferred, not measured.

industries.note: They would face compulsory licensing of patents for drugs judged overpriced or inadequately available, an annual audited disclosure of pricing and R&D costs, and cutoff from Medicare and Medicaid payments for missing the audit. Their exclusive-pricing model over the patent life would be directly limited.

Compulsory licenses would open a lawful channel to produce copies of patented medicines whose prices exceed federal criteria, with remuneration paid to the patent holder. Consumers would gain cheaper alternatives.

Any patentee of a health-related invention could see exclusivity overridden when its invention is unused, unneeded, or overpriced, but it would receive court-reviewed compensation and the bill expressly requires consistency with international patent rules.
